teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Both sentences give an order. Tap the order word in each — what do the two endings have in common?

teach.say: Beside the everyday order *venī!* (come, right now) Latin has **the future imperative (the 'you shall …' order for later or for rules: estō! mementō!)**. It gives an instruction for a time that has not come yet, or a rule that holds from now on: *crās venītō* — come tomorrow.

check.ask: Tap the word that gives the order.

teach.title: The singular ending: -tō
teach.say: Take the plain order you already use and add **-tō**: *amā* → *amātō*, *pārē* → *pārētō*, *lege* → *legitō*, *audī* → *audītō*. In the third conjugation the little vowel before the ending is *i*: *legitō* — the form this step's own sentence uses — and *scrībitō*, *mittitō*. The one form serves for 'you shall' and 'he shall' alike.

teach.title: The plural ending: -tōte
teach.say: For more than one person told to do it the ending is **-tōte**: *amātōte, pārētōte, scrībitōte, audītōte*. It is simply the singular *-tō* with *-te* on the end, just as the plain plural order *amāte* is *amā* with *-te*. An order about other people — 'they shall …' — ends in **-ntō** instead: *suntō*, *amantō*.

teach.title: The ones to learn by heart: estō, estōte, mementō, scītō
teach.say: *Sum* makes *estō* (you or he shall be) and *estōte* (you all shall be). Two more verbs are met almost only in this form: *mementō!* (remember) from *meminī*, and *scītō!* (know) from *sciō* — because remembering and knowing are states you are told to be in from now on, not acts you do this second.

check.ask: Write the future imperative singular of sum.

teach.title: Telling it from the plain imperative
teach.say: Both are orders, so the ending is the whole difference: *tacē* is 'be quiet this second', *respondētō* is 'answer when the time comes'. Watch one trap: *monitō* in *puerō monitō* is no order at all but a perfect participle in the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) agreeing with the noun beside it; *monētō*, with a long *ē*, is the order.

check.ask: One of these two orders is about later. Tap it.

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Use it where English says 'you shall', or where an instruction reaches forward — a letter telling the family what to do after they read it, a rule, a promise. It sits happily after a *cum* or *sī* clause about the future, because that is exactly the time it means.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the future imperative plural of pāreō.

core.text: Besides the everyday order (*pugnā!* fight!), Latin has **the future imperative (the 'you shall …' order for later or for rules: esto! memento!)**: *pugnātō!* — fight (when the time comes)! It ends in *-tō* (singular) and *-tōte* (plural) on the present stem: *amā-tō, monē-tō, scrībi-tō, audī-tō*; from *sum*: *estō, estōte*. It is the imperative (the command form) for instructions that hold from now on — laws, rules, letters saying what to do later — and a few fixed verbs: *mementō* (remember!), *scītō* (know that …). Latin name: *imperātīvus futūrī*.
English: *you shall not steal*; *be careful (from now on)*; *remember!* — orders about later or always, not about this very moment.
Present stem + -tō / -tōte (third person -tō / -ntō). It means about the same as the plain imperative, with a 'from now on / when that happens' colour.

*pugnā* (now!) and *pugnātō* (from now on / then) are both orders; Ørberg says they mean almost the same. Spot *-tō / -tōte*: that is the future one. *estō* is 'be (from now on)', *es* is 'be (right now)'.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *monitō* in *puerō monitō* (the boy having been warned, Week 2) is the perfect participle in the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form), agreeing with a noun; *monētō* with a long ē before *-tō* is 'warn!'. Check the vowel before *-tō* and whether the word agrees with a noun beside it.

The learner's notes have no page on this form. Ørberg's chapter 33 introduces it in three lines: *pugnātō, mīles! pugnātōte, mīlitēs!* — the future imperative ends in *-tō* (singular) and *-tōte* (plural) and means nearly the same as the present imperative *pugnā, pugnāte*. In the text Aemilius's letter home uses it for what his family should do after reading: *exspectātō, scrībitō, monētō, nārrātōte, scītōte*.

Allen & Greenough: the future imperative is used for orders whose carrying-out lies in the future, so it is the form of laws, wills and precepts (*rēgiō imperiō duo suntō* — let there be two with royal power), and of verbs that name a standing state: *mementō* (remember), *scītō* (know), *habētō* (consider). The third-person forms are *-tō* (singular, same as the second) and *-ntō* (plural); a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) uses *-tor* (*sequitor*). In laws the negative is *nē* + future imperative. The old-fashioned flavour is why it survives in mottoes (*estō perpetua*) and on tombstones.
Ørberg says the two mean nearly the same thing; the difference is the 'when the time comes' colouring.
